TTL (time to live) · vida de un paquete\:
TTL (time to live) · a packet's lifetime

Each IP packet carries a number, the TTL, set by its sender. Each router
forwarding it subtracts at least 1. If the result reaches 0, that router
discards it and notifies the source with an ICMP ‘time exceeded’ message.
This prevents packets from circling forever.

RFC 791 (1981) defined TTL in seconds: a router holding a packet in its queue
for N seconds subtracts N (never less than 1). RFC 1812 established the
practical rule followed by modern routers: always subtract 1.

Both rules coexist in the neighborhood Wired. The routing table gives each
router's queue time and rule. The sender does not count as a hop.

Segmentos, seq y len\n\nUn mensaje largo:
Segments, seq and len

A long message travels in segments. Each carries a sequence number
(seq: the byte where it starts in the message) and a length in bytes (len).
The next segment starts at seq + len. If a segment is lost or delayed,
it is retransmitted: copies may exist. The packet index (.idx) declares
each segment's correct sha256; an altered copy will not match.
sha256 <archivo> [línea] · huella de un:
sha256 <file> [line] · a content fingerprint

Computes the SHA-256 hash of the exact content (UTF-8) and displays its
first 8 hexadecimal characters. With a line number, it hashes that line
alone, without the newline. Changing a single character completely
changes the fingerprint.
Cadena de hashes · registros que no se p:
Hash chain · records cannot be silently rewritten

Each Wired journal entry stores in ‘prev’ the sha256 fingerprint of the
complete previous entry (the entire line as displayed). If someone rewrites
an entry, its fingerprint changes and no longer matches the next entry's
‘prev’. The break appears in the following entry; the forged entry is the
one before the break. Hiding a rewrite would require rebuilding the entire
subsequent chain, and someone with a copy would notice.

TCP · abrir una conexión (saludo de tres:
TCP · opening a connection (three-way handshake)

1. The caller sends SYN with its initial sequence number (seq=x).
2. The answering side sends SYN+ACK: its own initial number (seq=y) and ack=x+1,
   which means "I got your SYN; the next byte I expect is x+1".
3. The caller sends ACK with ack=y+1. The connection is ESTABLISHED.

A SYN uses up one sequence number even though it carries no data. If nobody
answers, the SYN is retransmitted with the same seq and the wait doubles.
A normal TCP stack answers by itself; the Navi's does not: send nodo07 SYN+ACK ...
ACK acumulativo\n\nack=n significa «he r:
Cumulative ACK

ack=n means "I have received everything up to byte n-1; I expect byte n".
You cannot confirm loose pieces: if a segment is missing, the ack stays at
the first missing byte even if later segments have arrived.
If you confirm bytes you do not have, the sender considers them delivered and

Retransmisión\n\nQuien envía guarda una:
Retransmission

The sender keeps a copy of everything not yet confirmed. It sends it again when
its timer expires (RTO: let time pass with wait) or, sooner, when it receives
three identical ACKs asking for the same byte: fast retransmit (RFC 5681).
Keepalive\n\nUna conexión sin datos pued:
Keepalive

A connection with no data can last forever if someone keeps it alive.
A keepalive is an empty segment with seq = next byte - 1 and the other side's
ack: it forces a reply without sending anything new (RFC 1122). That is why,
in a capture of keepalives, the connection's real next byte is seq + 1.
FIN · cerrar con cuidado\n\nCada lado ci:
FIN · closing gently

Each side closes its half. The closer sends FIN+ACK with its next seq and the
ack of what it has received; the other side confirms that FIN (ack = seq + 1)
and sends its own FIN; the closer confirms that FIN with a last ACK
(seq + 1, ack + 1) and stays in TIME_WAIT before CLOSED. A FIN uses up one
sequence number.
RST · cortar\n\nUn RST destruye la conex:
RST · cutting

An RST destroys the connection at once, without a goodbye. It is only accepted
if its seq is exactly the next byte the other side expects (RFC 5961).

Sesión\n\nUna sesión es el estado de alg:
Session

A session is someone's state while they are connected: who they are, what
they have done, what they remember. It expires after too long without
activity (idle timeout) and is archived. Restoring an expired session does not
make it the same one: it is its last saved state, loaded again.
Lease · arrendamiento\n\nPara que solo u:
Lease

So that only one session uses the account at a time, the system grants a
lease: an exclusive permission that expires. Whoever holds it is the holder;
if they stop renewing it, it expires and someone else can take it. Every grant
carries a number that only grows: the fencing token (man fencing).
Fencing token · token de exclusión\n\nUn:
Fencing token

An old holder may wake up late and believe it is still in charge. To prevent
that, every new lease brings a number higher than the previous one, and the
store rejects any write carrying a number lower than the last one it saw.
Only whoever presents the current token can write.
Versiones · concurrencia optimista\n\nCa:
Versions · optimistic concurrency

Every saved state has a version number. To write, you propose the version
after the one you read (compare-and-swap): if someone wrote first, the version
no longer matches and your write is rejected instead of overwriting theirs.
Fusión a tres bandas\n\nCuando dos versi:
Three-way merge

When two versions start from a common ancestor (base), each field is compared
with it:
  - if it changed in only one of them, that change wins;
  - if it changed the same way in both, there is no problem;
  - if it changed differently in both, there is a conflict and someone has to choose.
It is what git does when merging branches. merge <field> <base|s0|s1> picks
the value; merge with no arguments shows the merge in progress.

Codificación · bytes y texto\n\nUn archi:
Encoding · bytes and text

A file is bytes. To read them as text you need an encoding: in UTF-8, “a” is
the byte 61 and “á” is two bytes, c3 a1. Hexadecimal shows each byte as two
digits, from 00 to ff. Base64 writes any byte with 64 safe characters
(A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) so it can travel over text channels: every 3 bytes take 4
characters. Encoding is not encrypting: anyone can undo it.

you need a signature (man hmac).

Señal · niveles en un cable\n\nPor un ca:
Signal · levels on a cable

Bits do not travel down a cable; voltage levels that change over time do. An
oscilloscope samples them: it measures the level many times per second and
draws high (¯) or low (_). If the line runs at 10 Mbit/s with Manchester, it
changes level up to 20 million times per second (20 Mbaud). Sampling at
60 MS/s gives 3 samples for each half-bit.
Codificación Manchester\n\nCada bit ocup:
Manchester encoding

Each bit takes two half-bits with a transition in the middle, so the receiver
recovers the clock from the signal itself. In IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet 10BASE-T),
a 1 is low→high and a 0 is high→low. The G. E. Thomas convention is the
opposite. If a pair has its wires crossed, the signal arrives inverted and
reads with the opposite convention. Two equal half-bits are a code violation.
Ruido · votación por mayoría\n\nEl ruido:
Noise · majority vote

Noise flips individual samples. If each half-bit has several samples, the
majority decides: with 3 samples, two equal ones win. That is why you sample
faster than the signal. If you pick the wrong number of samples per half-bit,
the groups slip out of line and code violations appear everywhere.
Preámbulo y SFD\n\nToda trama Ethernet e:
Preamble and SFD

Every Ethernet frame starts with 7 bytes of 0x55 (10101010 on the wire) so the
receiver can synchronise, and a 0xD5 byte (SFD, start frame delimiter) that
marks the real start. Ethernet sends each byte least significant bit first. If
decoding gives 0xAA instead of 0x55, the bits are inverted.
Cable de par trenzado\n\n10BASE-T usa do:
Twisted pair cable

10BASE-T uses two pairs: orange (naranja, pins 1-2) to transmit and green
(verde, pins 3-6) to receive. Each pair carries the signal on two wires with
opposite voltages; if they are crossed, the polarity flips. A pair with no data
only carries link pulses (NLP), an isolated spike every 16 ms, to say “still
here”.
